nameStory: The 'smoky' in Smoky Crottle refers to this lichen's distinctive blue-gray to smoky gray color that becomes more pronounced when wet. 'Crottle' is an old Scottish and Irish word for lichens that were traditionally used to dye wool, producing beautiful purple, red, and brown colors that made them valuable to textile makers.
description: Smoky Crottle is a leafy, flat-growing lichen that forms spreading patches on rocks and tree bark. It has a distinctive blue-gray to smoky gray color that becomes more vibrant when moistened by rain or morning dew. The lichen grows in rosette-like patterns with lobed edges that can spread several inches across, creating attractive circular or irregular patches that look almost painted onto their surface.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Blue-gray to smoky gray color that becomes noticeably more vibrant and bluish when wet, fading to pale gray when completely dry

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Foliose (leafy) with flat, overlapping lobes that spread outward in rosette-like patterns, feeling papery and flexible when damp

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Smooth to slightly wrinkled upper surface that feels thin and delicate, with a white to pale underside visible at the edges

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Found on both acidic rock surfaces and tree bark, particularly favoring exposed locations with good air circulation

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches can spread 2-6 inches across, with lobes typically 1/4 to 1/2 inch wide

habitat: Look for Smoky Crottle on exposed rocks, boulders, and tree trunks throughout New England's forests and rocky areas. It particularly favors acidic substrates and can be found from sea level to mountain elevations, often in areas with good air quality. You'll spot it on everything from granite outcrops to the bark of oak and maple trees in both deciduous and mixed forests.

seasonality.spring: Spring rains bring out the vibrant blue-gray colors beautifully, making this an excellent time for identification as the lichen stays moist longer in the cool, humid conditions.
seasonality.summer: During dry summer periods, the lichen appears much paler and grayer, but thunderstorms will quickly revive its distinctive smoky blue tones within minutes of getting wet.
seasonality.fall: Fall's frequent rains and morning dews keep the lichen colorful and make it easy to spot against autumn's changing backdrop, particularly on tree bark.
seasonality.winter: Snow and ice can temporarily hide specimens, but winter thaws reveal the lichen in its full smoky glory, often appearing almost luminous against dark, wet rock surfaces.

funFact: This ancient lichen was one of the very first lichens ever scientifically described - way back in 1753 by Carl Linnaeus himself, the same botanist who created our modern system of naming plants and animals, making it literally one of the founding species of lichen science!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other gray shield lichens, but Smoky Crottle's distinctive blue-gray color when wet is the key - other similar species tend toward pure gray or greenish-gray. Memory trick: 'Blue when wet, smoky when dry' helps distinguish it from its cousins.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'shield lichen,' this species is actually quite delicate compared to some of its more robust relatives. The traditional use of crottles for dyeing wool was so important in Scotland and Ireland that specific recipes were closely guarded family secrets passed down through generations.
compareHints: Unlike Netted Shield Lichen which has a distinctly white, net-like pattern on its surface, or Bottlebrush Shield Lichen with its fuzzy, hair-like projections, Smoky Crottle has a relatively smooth surface. It lacks the salt-and-pepper appearance of Salted Shield Lichen and has much more pronounced blue tones when wet than any of its shield lichen relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Netted shield lichen is distinguished from its shield lichen relatives by its unique white net pattern - bottlebrush shield lichen has tiny finger-like projections, while salted shield lichen has a more uniformly smooth surface with white spots rather than a connected network.

Bottlebrush shield lichen stands out from other Parmelia species by its distinctive branching edge projections - netted shield lichen has a more reticulated (net-like) surface pattern, while salted shield lichen has simpler, less ornate edges.
Unlike its cousin the Netted Shield Lichen which has raised white ridges forming a net pattern, Salted Shield Lichen has scattered granular patches.
Among the shield lichens, fertile shield lichen is distinguished by its pale, prominent pores and frequent fruiting body production.
